summary: Updates RFC 7519 with practical guidance for implementing and deploying JSON Web Tokens securely. JWTs are widely used signed or encrypted tokens carrying claims, in digital identity and other areas, and this best current practice document describes how to avoid known pitfalls.

plainLanguage.summary: A JSON Web Token is a signed or encrypted note that a service can check. This document lists the ways attackers have fooled real services into accepting a forged token, and the checks that stop them.

questions: what is the jwt alg none attack
subtitle: The rules for checking a JWT before you trust it, written after a series of real attacks on JWT deployments.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Tokens have been widely published as easy to use and hard to get wrong, but several attacks have succeeded against real deployments. Most come from the same causes: the token says which algorithm it uses, and the receiver believed it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8725 lists the known attacks, then gives a floor of practices: pin the algorithm, validate every cryptographic operation and input, use strong keys, do not compress, check issuer, subject and audience, and give each kind of token its own explicit type.
tldr.outcome: A receiver following the rules rejects tokens that are unsigned, weakly keyed, for the wrong audience or of the wrong kind. It is a Best Current Practice from February 2020 that updates RFC 7519 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8725 is a Best Current Practice published in February 2020. It updates RFC 7519, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
JSON Web Tokens, also known as JWTs, are URL-safe JSON-based security tokens that contain a set of claims that can be signed and/or encrypted. The JWT specification has seen rapid adoption because it encapsulates security-relevant information in one easy-to-protect location, and because it is easy to implement using widely available tools. One application area in which JWTs are commonly used is representing digital identity information, such as OpenID Connect ID Tokens and OAuth 2.0 access tokens and refresh tokens.

Since the JWT specification was published, there have been several widely published attacks on implementations and deployments. Such attacks are the result of under-specified security mechanisms, as well as incomplete implementations and incorrect usage by applications. The goal of this document is to facilitate secure implementation and deployment of JWTs. Many of the recommendations are about implementation and use of the cryptographic mechanisms defined by JSON Web Signature, JSON Web Encryption and JSON Web Algorithms; others are about use of the JWT claims themselves.

These are intended to be minimum recommendations for the vast majority of implementation and deployment scenarios. Other specifications that reference this document can have stricter requirements, and this document provides a floor, not a ceiling, so stronger options are always allowed. Community knowledge about the strength of various algorithms and feasible attacks can change quickly, and experience shows that a Best Current Practice document about security is a point-in-time statement.
sections.plainLanguage: JWTs became popular quickly, and attackers followed. Most of the trouble comes from the token carrying its own name of the algorithm used, and the checker believing whatever it says.

sections.title: Attacks That Have Worked
sections.content:
Signed tokens carry an explicit indication of the signing algorithm, in the form of the alg header parameter, to facilitate cryptographic agility. In conjunction with design flaws in some libraries and applications, this has led to several attacks. The algorithm can be changed to none by an attacker, and some libraries would trust this value and validate the JWT without checking any signature. An RS256 parameter value, RSA with a 2048-bit key, can be changed into HS256, HMAC with SHA-256, and some libraries would try to validate the signature using HMAC-SHA256 and using the RSA public key as the HMAC shared secret.

Some applications use a keyed message authentication code algorithm such as HS256 to sign tokens but supply a weak symmetric key with insufficient entropy, such as a human-memorable password. Such keys are vulnerable to offline brute-force or dictionary attacks once an attacker gets hold of such a token.

Some libraries that decrypt an encrypted JWT to obtain a signed object do not always validate the internal signature. Many encryption algorithms leak information about the length of the plaintext, and this problem is exacerbated when the plaintext is initially compressed, because the length of the compressed plaintext depends not only on the length of the original plaintext but also on its content. Compression attacks are particularly powerful when there is attacker-controlled data in the same compression space as secret data.

Several JOSE libraries fail to validate their inputs correctly when performing elliptic curve key agreement with the ECDH-ES algorithm. An attacker able to send JWEs using invalid curve points and observe the cleartext outputs can use this to recover the recipient's private key.

Older JSON standards allowed several character encodings, UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32, and older implementations or those used within closed environments may still generate non-standard encodings, which may result in the JWT being misinterpreted by its recipient and used by a malicious sender to bypass the recipient's validation checks.

Substitution attacks give one recipient a JWT intended for it, which it then tries to use at a different recipient for which the JWT was not intended, for example an OAuth 2.0 access token presented to one protected resource and then passed on to another. Cross-JWT confusion is the specific case where a JWT issued for one purpose is subverted and used for another.

Finally, various JWT claims are used by the recipient to perform lookup operations, such as database and LDAP searches, and others include URLs that are similarly looked up. Any of these claims can be used by an attacker as vectors for injection attacks or server-side request forgery attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacks fall into a few families: changing the algorithm name to something weaker, using a password as a key, forgetting to check the inner signature, leaking length through compression, accepting bad curve points, and passing a token on to the wrong service.

sections.title: Pin Down the Algorithm
sections.content:
Libraries MUST enable the caller to specify a supported set of algorithms and MUST NOT use any other algorithms when performing cryptographic operations. The library MUST ensure that the alg or enc header specifies the same algorithm that is used for the cryptographic operation. Each key MUST be used with exactly one algorithm, and this MUST be checked when the cryptographic operation is performed.

Applications MUST only allow the use of cryptographically current algorithms that meet the security requirements of the application. This set will vary over time as new algorithms are introduced and existing ones deprecated, so applications MUST be designed to enable cryptographic agility.

If a JWT is cryptographically protected end to end by a transport layer, such as TLS using current algorithms, there may be no need to apply another layer of protection to the JWT, and the use of the none algorithm can be perfectly acceptable. The none algorithm should only be used when the JWT is cryptographically protected by other means. JWT libraries SHOULD NOT generate or consume JWTs using none unless explicitly requested to do so by the caller.

The RFC also gives algorithm-specific advice. Avoid all RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption algorithms, preferring RSAES-OAEP. ECDSA signatures require a unique random value for every message that is signed, and if even a few bits of the random value are predictable across multiple messages the security of the signature scheme may be compromised, so JWT libraries SHOULD implement ECDSA using the deterministic approach defined in RFC 6979, which is completely compatible with existing ECDSA verifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Decide in advance which algorithms you accept, and reject anything else. The name inside the token is a hint, not a decision, and a key should be tied to one algorithm only.

sections.title: Validate Every Cryptographic Step
sections.content:
All cryptographic operations used in the JWT MUST be validated, and the entire JWT MUST be rejected if any of them fail to validate. This is true not only of JWTs with a single set of header parameters but also for nested JWTs, in which both outer and inner operations MUST be validated using the keys and algorithms supplied by the application.

Some cryptographic operations, such as elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement, take inputs that may contain invalid values, including points not on the specified elliptic curve. The library itself must validate these inputs before using them, or use underlying cryptographic libraries that do so. ECDH-ES ephemeral public key inputs should be validated according to the recipient's chosen elliptic curve. For the NIST prime-order curves P-256, P-384 and P-521, validation MUST be performed according to the ECC Partial Public-Key Validation Routine of NIST Special Publication 800-56A Revision 3. If the X25519 or X448 algorithms are used, the security considerations in RFC 8037 apply.

The key entropy and random values advice in RFC 7515 and the password considerations in RFC 7518 MUST be followed. Human-memorizable passwords MUST NOT be directly used as the key to a keyed-MAC algorithm such as HS256. Passwords should only be used to perform key encryption rather than content encryption, and even when used for key encryption, password-based encryption is still subject to brute-force attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Check every layer, not just the outer one, and check the maths too: a point that is not on the curve must be rejected before it is used. Never sign with a password.

sections.title: Do Not Compress, and Use UTF-8
sections.content:
Compression of data SHOULD NOT be done before encryption, because such compressed data often reveals information about the plaintext. The length of the ciphertext then depends on the content of the plaintext and not just its length, and compression attacks are particularly powerful when there is attacker-controlled data in the same compression space as secret data.

RFC 7515, RFC 7516 and RFC 7519 all specify that UTF-8 be used for encoding and decoding JSON used in header parameters and JWT claims sets, and this is in line with the latest JSON specification. Implementations and applications MUST do this and not use or admit the use of other Unicode encodings for these purposes, since older implementations and those used within closed environments may generate non-standard encodings that the recipient misinterprets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two small rules with real consequences: do not compress before encrypting, and accept only UTF-8, so that the same token cannot be read two different ways.

sections.title: Check Issuer, Subject and Audience
sections.content:
When a JWT contains an iss issuer claim, the application MUST validate that the cryptographic keys used for the cryptographic operations in the JWT belong to the issuer, and if they do not it MUST reject the JWT. The means of determining the keys owned by an issuer is application-specific: OpenID Connect issuer values are https URLs that reference a JSON metadata document containing a jwks_uri value, an https URL from which the issuer's keys are retrieved as a JWK Set.

Similarly, when the JWT contains a sub subject claim, the application MUST validate that the subject value corresponds to a valid subject and/or issuer-subject pair at the application, and if the issuer, subject or the pair are invalid it MUST reject the JWT.

If the same issuer can issue JWTs intended for more than one relying party or application, the JWT MUST contain an aud audience claim, and the relying party MUST validate the audience value. If the audience value is not present or not associated with the recipient, it MUST reject the JWT.

Received claims should not be trusted for lookups. The kid header is used to perform key lookup, and applications should validate or sanitise the received value so that it does not create SQL or LDAP injection vulnerabilities. Blindly following a jku or x5u header, which may contain an arbitrary URL, could result in server-side request forgery attacks; applications SHOULD protect against such attacks, for example by matching the URL to a whitelist of allowed locations and ensuring no cookies are sent in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: Check who sent the token, who it is about, and who it is for. And treat everything inside the token as text to be checked, not as a command to follow.

sections.title: Make Different Kinds of Token Unmixable
sections.content:
Sometimes one kind of JWT can be confused for another. If a particular kind of JWT is subject to such confusion, it can include an explicit JWT type value and the validation rules can specify checking the type. Explicit typing is accomplished by using the typ header parameter. For instance, RFC 8417 uses the application/secevent+jwt media type to perform explicit typing of Security Event Tokens. It is RECOMMENDED that the application/ prefix be omitted from the typ value, so the type value used to explicitly include a type for a Security Event Token SHOULD be secevent+jwt. When explicit typing is employed for a JWT, it is RECOMMENDED that a media type name of the format application/example+jwt be used, where example is replaced by the identifier for the specific kind of JWT. When applying explicit typing to a nested JWT, the typ header parameter containing the explicit type value MUST be present in the inner JWT.

Each application of JWTs defines a profile specifying the required and optional claims and the validation rules associated with them. If more than one kind of JWT can be issued by the same issuer, the validation rules for those JWTs MUST be written so that they are mutually exclusive, rejecting JWTs of the wrong kind. The RFC lists six strategies: use explicit typing; use different sets of required claims or different required claim values; use different sets of required header parameters or different required header parameter values; use different keys for different kinds of JWTs; use different audience values for different uses from the same issuer; and use different issuers for different kinds of JWTs.
sections.plainLanguage: If one server hands out several kinds of token, make them impossible to swap. You can label the token with its type, require different claims, use different keys, or use a different audience or issuer for each kind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This entire document is about security considerations when implementing and deploying JSON Web Tokens. The RFC states that it has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Every recommendation in this document is a security measure, and nothing here changes the registries.

items.title: Algorithm changed to none
items.text: Some libraries accept an unsigned token as valid.

items.title: RS256 changed to HS256
items.text: The RSA public key is used as the HMAC shared secret.

items.title: Weak signing key
items.text: A human-memorable password used as a MAC key can be cracked offline.

items.title: Inner signature not checked
items.text: A decrypted token's signature is sometimes skipped.

items.title: Compression leaks length
items.text: Compressed ciphertext length depends on the plaintext content.

items.title: Invalid curve points
items.text: Bad ECDH-ES inputs can reveal the recipient's private key.

cells: Pin the accepted algorithms and check the header matches
Use exactly one algorithm per key and check it
Use keys with enough entropy, never a password
Validate every operation, inner and outer
Validate elliptic curve inputs before use
Validate the audience and use explicit typing

items.title: Algorithm
items.text: Only algorithms you chose in advance, one per key.

items.title: Every operation
items.text: Validate all of them, and reject the whole token if one fails.

items.title: Inputs
items.text: Check that curve points and other inputs are valid.

items.title: Keys
items.text: Enough entropy, and never a human-memorable password.

items.title: Encoding
items.text: UTF-8 only, and no compression before encryption.

items.title: Claims
items.text: Check issuer, subject and audience, and treat lookups as untrusted input.
